**February 29, 1960 — a Monday**

Before anything else: you were born on a day the calendar omits in three out of every four years. That mathematical fact deserves a moment.

**The arithmetic of your life:** In 66 years, February 29 has appeared exactly 16 times — 1964, 1968, and every fourth year through 2024. Your 15th actual birthday fell in 2020, in the early weeks of a global pandemic that had not yet fully declared itself. Your 16th was 2024. The next is 2028. Everyone born in February 1960 has had 66 birthdays; you have had 16. The next person you meet who shares your exact birthday — not just the year, but the day — was born once every four years alongside you, a cohort so small it fits in a modest room.

**The exact day — Agadir vanishes:** In the early hours of February 29, 1960, an earthquake struck directly beneath the Moroccan city of Agadir. It measured roughly magnitude 5.7 — not extraordinary by seismic standards — but it was shallow and centered under a dense urban area. The result was catastrophic: approximately 12,000 people killed in seconds, roughly a third of the city's population gone overnight. Agadir had to be abandoned and rebuilt from scratch on a different footprint. The disaster was a lesson in how vulnerability concentrates — not just in fault lines, but in construction quality, in poverty, in where cities are built and why. The world received that lesson the day you arrived in it.

**Twenty-six days before your birth — the wind of change:** On February 3, 1960, British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan stood before the South African parliament in Cape Town and said: "The wind of change is blowing through this continent." He was telling the white minority government directly that African independence was inevitable and that Britain would not stand behind apartheid. It was a signal that the colonial order was ending — and that Britain understood this even if South Africa did not.

**Your birth year as Africa's year:** 1960 is known as the Year of Africa. Seventeen nations gained independence from European colonial powers in a single calendar year — among them Nigeria, Senegal, Mali, the Congo, Cameroon, Somalia, and Ivory Coast. The map of the continent was being redrawn month by month. You were born at the hinge point of that transformation, when the colonial world that had organized global power for a century was visibly giving way to something not yet fully defined.

**Twenty-one days after your birth — Sharpeville:** On March 21, 1960, South African police opened fire on Black protesters in Sharpeville who were demonstrating against the pass laws. Sixty-nine people were killed, most shot in the back as they fled. The massacre drew global condemnation, transformed international understanding of apartheid, and set South Africa on the path toward decades of isolation — a path that wouldn't end until Nelson Mandela walked free in 1990, when you were 30 years old. You were three weeks old when the event that defined that struggle happened.

**Two and a half months after your birth — the pill:** On May 9, 1960, the FDA approved Enovid, the first oral contraceptive pill, for contraceptive use. You were born 10 weeks before the approval of a technology that would fundamentally alter the social organization of the second half of the twentieth century — reshaping women's education, careers, family structure, and expectations in ways that are still working themselves out. The world your mother inhabited and the world you grew up in were separated by, among other things, that single regulatory decision.

**The arc of 66 years:** You were 3 when Kennedy was shot. You were 9 when humans walked on the moon. You were 29 when the Berlin Wall fell, ending the Cold War that had been present for your entire conscious life. You were 41 on September 11, 2001. You've watched the world reorganize itself around forces — decolonization, women's liberation, digital communication, climate — that were just beginning to take shape the February you arrived.

The Monday you were born doesn't appear on most calendars. Neither does the world you were born into — the one with Agadir intact, Africa still mapped in colonial colors, the pill not yet approved, the wind of change still blowing. That world is as gone as February 29 is on most years: present once, then absent, then present again in altered form.
